clinicalPearls: Exercise-induced pain along the posteromedial border of the tibia, typically over a diffuse length rather than a focal point
Pain characteristically eases with rest early on but can become more persistent with continued activity
It is an overuse injury common in runners, dancers and military recruits, often after a change in training load or surface
A key differential is tibial stress fracture, which causes more focal tenderness and pain, and chronic exertional compartment syndrome
Tenderness is spread over several centimetres of the distal medial tibia, unlike the pinpoint tenderness of a stress fracture
Management centres on relative rest, load modification, addressing biomechanical and training factors, and graded return
reference.pathophysiology: Medial tibial stress syndrome represents a bone-stress and periosteal overload injury along the posteromedial tibia, sitting on a continuum that can progress to tibial stress fracture. Repetitive loading exceeds the bone's capacity to remodel, producing periosteal and cortical stress and traction from the muscles attaching along the tibial border. Contributing factors include training errors, poor footwear, hard surfaces and biomechanical abnormalities such as overpronation, which concentrate load on the medial tibia.
additionalDifferentials: Tendinopathy of tibialis posterior or soleus
Nerve entrapment causing exertional leg pain
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the diffuse posteromedial tibial tenderness
Plain radiographs, often normal, to exclude other bony pathology
MRI or bone scan where stress fracture needs to be distinguished
Assessment of training load, footwear and biomechanics
Compartment pressure testing if exertional compartment syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Focal tenderness and night or rest pain suggesting stress fracture
Neurovascular symptoms suggesting compartment syndrome or arterial entrapment
Failure to improve with appropriate load management
Features suggesting bone pathology other than stress injury
reference.prognosis: The condition usually resolves with load modification and correction of contributing factors, though recovery can be slow and recurrence is common if training errors persist.
pitfalls: Missing a progressing tibial stress fracture
Overlooking chronic exertional compartment syndrome as the true cause
Returning to full training too quickly
Failing to correct biomechanical and training-load factors
management: Relative rest and load modification, reducing the aggravating running or impact volume
Correct contributing factors: training errors, running surface, appropriate footwear and orthoses for overpronation
Symptomatic relief with ice and simple analgesia
Rehabilitation with calf and lower-limb strengthening and gait retraining
Graded, progressive return to impact loading once symptoms settle
Monitor for progression to tibial stress fracture and image if focal pain develops
Refer for specialist assessment in refractory cases, with surgery such as posterior fasciotomy or periosteal release rarely required
